subtopic: Reaching a toy on a shelf
passage: Monday: Eshaan stood under the low shelf, rose onto tiptoe and reached for the stuffed elephant with one arm, grunting. The fingers stopped short. Ujjwal, Eshaan's father, watched from the sofa. Wednesday: Eshaan swapped arms and stretched with the other hand, wobbling. Still short. Saturday: same shelf, same tiptoes, and the elephant's ear finally brushed a fingertip and slid an inch closer. Ujjwal hid a smile and did not step in.

qa.q: What did Eshaan reach for on the shelf?
qa.a: Eshaan reached for the stuffed elephant.

qa.q: What might Eshaan be feeling as the fingers stop short again on Wednesday?
qa.a: Eshaan is probably frustrated but determined; the grunting and the switch to the other arm show effort and a wish to succeed.

qa.q: What different approach could work if stretching keeps falling short, and why?
qa.a: Eshaan could pull over a small stool with a grown-up close by, or ask Ujjwal for help, because added height or a helper solves what a longer stretch cannot.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal see Eshaan's plan?
qa.a: Ujjwal sees steady effort worth letting play out, so he holds back and smiles, even though he could lift the elephant down at any moment.

grounding: A toddler under a low shelf stretches up on tiptoe with one arm, then the other, for a stuffed elephant.

subtopic: Reaching a toy on a shelf
passage: Karthik spotted his grey stuffed elephant on the lowest shelf of the bookcase in their tenth-floor Pune flat, just above his head. He padded over, rose onto his toes and pushed his right arm up, grunting. His fingertips brushed the wood and slid off. He dropped back, swapped, and reached up with his left hand instead, face scrunched tight. His big sister Ankita looked up from her homework. "Almost, Karthik!"

qa.q: Which hand did Karthik try after his right arm fell short?
qa.a: He reached up with his left hand instead.

qa.q: What does Karthik's scrunched face suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: He seems determined and a bit frustrated: the first reach failed, but he grunts and keeps going with the other hand.

qa.q: What else could Karthik try when stretching is not enough?
qa.a: He could point at the elephant and look to Ankita for help, because asking reaches further than his arm can.

qa.q: How does Ankita see her little brother's effort?
qa.a: She finds it endearing and wants to encourage him, so she cheers because he is so close.

grounding: A toddler rises on tiptoe to reach a toy on a shelf and switches to the other hand when the first reach falls short.

subtopic: Reaching a toy on a shelf
passage:
"Payal, what are you doing up there, jaan?" her mother Dilnaz called from the kitchen door.
"Ellie!" Payal jabbed a finger at the shelf, then went up on her toes. "Nnngh!"
"Your elephant? It's high today, na?"
Payal's left hand slapped the shelf edge, a finger short. "Uh!" She swapped, flinging her right hand higher.
"Other hand now? Still not there?"
"Ellie!" Payal wailed, straining again.
Dilnaz knelt beside her. "Shall we try together?"

qa.q: What name does Payal use for her elephant?
What was Payal feeling when she wailed "Ellie!" and strained again?
qa.a: She was frustrated and eager at once: she wanted the elephant badly, and both hands had come up short.

qa.q: Which approach would suit Payal better now, and why?
qa.a: Letting Dilnaz help, or asking with a point and a look, would work better, because her arms simply are not long enough yet.

qa.q: If you were Dilnaz, what would you want for Payal here?
qa.a: You would want her to keep trying but not end up in tears, so offering to try together gives help without taking over.

grounding: A toddler stretches on tiptoe toward a toy, trying one hand and then the other, while her mother comments and offers help.
